newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North and South Korea head for new showdown.
newsitem.headline: North and South Korea head for new showdown.

text.p: South and North Korea on Wednesday headed for a dangerous new showdown over the fate of one of the communist countrys top ideologues who Seoul said wants to defect and Pyongyang suspects was kidnapped.
Caught in the middle was China, one of Stalinish North Koreas few allies.

South Korea said Hwang Jang-yop, 73, a senior adviser to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il and one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of the Workers Party, was in Seouls Beijing embassy along with an aide seeking asylum.
Hwang is also a member of the partys central committee and is in charge of its foreign policy, according to Seoul officials who rank him number 24 in the Pyongyang power structure.
North Korea said Hwangs defection was inconceivable and called on China to take appropriate measures "if it is brought to light that South Korean authorities kidnapped him."
The row broke just as ties between the commnist and capitalist foes were stabilising after a North Korean submarine incursion last year into South Korean waters.
The drama between two nations which fought the 1950-1953 Korean War and have been at each others throat ever since was played out as each went through their own internal crises.
After two years of floods, North Korea is in economic ruin appealing for international aid to stave off a killer famine.

The possible defection of the highest-ever North Korean official to the south broke four days before Kim celebrates his 55th birthday in ceremonies meant to position him to take over unchallenged leadership of the ailing nation later in the year.
Kim, the norths defacto leader since the death of his father in July, 1994, still has to claim the titles of communist party leader and head of state.
In Seoul, President Kim Young-sam faced his own political challenge as a loans scandal involving the failed Hanbo Steel Co claimed its first cabinet victim, one of the presidents most trusted aides.
Home Affairs Minister Kim Woo-suk offered his resignation hours before prosecutors began grilling him on whether he took kickbacks to secure loans for Hanbo.
Hanbo Steel managed to wring $6 billion of loans from the financial system when it had a net worth of just $300 million.

Another Kim Young-sam lieutenant, Hwang Byung-tai, was also questioned by prosecutors as a probe into what is shaping up as South Koreas biggest corporate scandal further eroded the presidents credibility.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung made known he was ready to resign to try to take responsibility for the scandal and limit damage to the government.

For the United States, desperate to keep stability on the Korean Peninsula where it has tens of thousands of troops based, the sudden woes of the two leaders were a setback to its efforts to get peace talks started between them.

In Tokyo, North Korea expert Masao Okonogi said a defection could pour cold water on expectations in Washington and Seoul that North Korea will agree to join them and China in four-way talks aimed at achieving a permanent peace on the Korean peninsula.
"It may be difficult to hold the four-way talks," Okonogi said. "His defection says to the international community that a very senior official has given up on the future of North Korea."
